chunks.text: Right. Now we're in... We're in public. We're in public. Okay, we're in public on this one. Right, cool. Right, great. Thank you very much for the response that you've given us. Right, cool So, good morning chair and members of the committee. My name is Robyn Elston, I'm the National Manager of Local Government at NZTA Waka Kotahi, and we appreciate the opportunity to appear before the committee regarding the petition of Free Fares New Zealand, stop the proposed public transport fare hikes.

I'd like to start by directly addressing the central concern raised in the petition. NZTA recognizes that fare increases can affect affordability and can be challenging for some public transport users, particularly during a period of ongoing cost of living pressures. We also recognize the important role public transport plays in supporting access to work, education, healthcare, and community participation, as well as its contribution to reducing congestion and supporting environmental outcomes.

However, public transport services must also be financially sustainable. Over recent years, the proportion of public transport operating costs funded through private revenue has fallen significantly. National private share was approximately 33% in 2018/2019, and had declined to 10% by 2022/23. As private share declined, a greater proportion of operating costs was funded by taxpayers and ratepayers. In response to GPS and Land Transport 24 setting the expectation that public transport authorities work towards increasing private share over time, and NZTA's

role is to implement that direction. It is important to be clear about what NZTA does and does not do. NZTA does not set public transport fares, determine concession policies, or decide local service levels. Except for SuperGold and Community Connect, which are set by the government, the remaining transport fares concession policy decisions remain the responsibility of public transport authorities and their elected representatives. NZTA has not directed councils to implement specific fare increases.

Our role has been to work alongside public transport authorities to establish appropriate targets and support them in identifying how those targets can be achieved. When developing those targets, NZTA engaged extensively with public transport authorities across the country. Following that engagement, the final targets were approved by the NZTA board, and they were lower than those that were originally proposed and were tailored to regional circumstances.

NZTA also encouraged authorities to consider approaches that avoided adverse outcomes, such as significant patronage decline. Ultimately, we do not see this as a choice between affordable public transport and sustainable public transport. The challenge is finding the right balance between affordability, patronage growth, environmental objectives, and long-term funding sustainability.

And NZTA's role is to support that balance while implementing the expectations set by government through GPS '24. Thank you. Thank you, Robyn. We've questions. We're good for questions? Yes. Okay, right. Cool. Who's going to kick us off? Julianne? Thanks so much, Robyn. I'm just wondering if you can confirm that the rationale that you just gave for having a policy to get a greater share of funding from private share in a very short term is something that was set by the government.

It's a policy decision set by the government of the day. It's not a rationale that maybe would exist independently. Like if you went out to other places, other cities, other countries, this isn't an approach that is necessarily deemed the best approach from a public policy point of view.

We were implementing the GPS. Yeah. And that was a choice, a political choice. Thanks. To what degree that was driven by reductions in fares, and obviously there was some very temporary reductions in fares through COVID, et cetera, which were clearly one-offs.

Yeah. And then to what extent it was driven by increases in the cost of the services. We've got quite a number of things, the change to the PTOM model, increase in remuneration. I'm not sure if the move to electric buses will do it because that's long-term. Chair, it's a mix. The cost of providing public transport has gone up. It's around about 4%, I think, per year in terms of costs going up, and fares have not increased. PTAs have not significantly increased fares over that period. So they're absorbing more costs.

And changes to half-price fares and those and concessions have all played their role because it's a balance between- Okay. About 4%, though, that's a useful thing. What was the sort of nature of concerns that were expressed by authorities around the ability to achieve that? Sure. regional council focus in that one, and also trying to balance the effect of... So increase in private share does not automatically mean an increase in public, in fares. But you would've seen that there was an original proposal around the extent that private share should increase, and that was changed as a result of the conversations with the PTA. So that would suggest that there was some challenges that NZTA took on board and the NZTA board took on board.

We can provide the committee with that information Okay. But if you haven't increased fees over a certain period, you would be looking at patronage and costs as a way of managing to ensure that you had a sustainable public transport service.

Sure. Cool. Are there any other questions? Okay, so just in terms of this, we will have to write a report in due course. But obviously, there's some information we've asked you to bring back. So if we can do that, what sort of timeframe to be able to bring that back? It shouldn't be hard. Sorry?

It shouldn't be hard. We can do it in a week, two weeks. Yeah. Okay. Well, let's aim for next week, and then we can get a report done. Yeah. But very much appreciated. Morning. Morning. Thank you for being here. No, this one is in- Morning. Okay. Right. So what we're going to do is we've had correspondence. Thank you for responding to the summons. And I think what I'm going to do is go straight, if you're okay with that, straight to questions.

Sure. Okay. Thanks. Sure. Thank you. And thank you both for coming in. And thank you for the correspondence that you've given to the committee. You'll recall back in early December, I asked a number of questions that related to the former employment of Mr. Dewatna.

Mm-hmm. Looking at the transcript, there were three specific occasions that you as chief executive indicated that you would come back to the committee with that. Do you accept that that commitment was made to the committee? Yes, absolutely. Yes, okay. When was the decision made to ultimately not release that information to the committee?

I think in that committee meeting, Kane had said that we'd take advice and then come back to you. And the facts that we did not are not in dispute, and we've extended an apology for that on the 6th of May in writing. The media also had significant interest in that that day and the following day, and we did put out some public commentary that we were unable to make any comments regarding that.

We then followed up with Mr. Dewatna in person. We did receive his permission to waive his privacy on it, and we did go out publicly to state the nature of his settlement payment. And if I can add to that, I don't think there was a decision not to provide the committee with information. The sequence of events was, we'd committed to take some further advice on what information we could share with the committee, which we did.

Between the committee hearing and the written request for further information from the committee, which I think was later in December just before Christmas, we had received a number of OIA requests from media outlets, particularly in relation to the details around the arrangements with Mr. Dewatna, which we had provided. So we had assumed wrongly, with the benefit of hindsight, that when the committee had followed up with subsequent requests for information, which didn't include information about Mr.

Dewatna's arrangements, that because it had been in the public domain, there wasn't any need to provide any further information. That's why I think in the letter that we'd responded, we said actually we've made some changes to our process, which is if we've made the commitment to get back to the committee, particularly in a case like this, what ought to have happened is that we should have provided that information to the committee as we were responding to official information requests.

I'm pleased to hear that. I guess we have a circumstance here where in the committee's own letter to you, it has formed the view that the behavior and conduct of the CAA is highly disrespectful to parliamentary proceedings. And so I guess we're interested, well, I'm interested in what specifically has been put in place with the authority to ensure that if a parliamentary select committee undertaking an annual review of your organization has asked you specific questions, and then to read about those answers in the media,

that is highly disrespectful. So what specifically has been put in place to ensure that that will not happen again? So the process we have in place now, so obviously we'll have an annual review hearing coming up in a few months, is that if there are questions that come out of the committee where we've made a commitment to come back, we will progress those commitments rather than wait for the committee to provide us follow-up questions.

As I said, if I was to rerun what ought to have happened in this case, if we were to put that new process in place, we would provide the information that ultimately leaked to the public to this committee at the time or prior to that information going out in the public domain. Mr. Derrick, as chair, when were you made aware that the commitment to this committee had not been fulfilled?

When I received a letter. From the committee? That's right. On the 30th of April. So you were here at the start of December when this exchange took place, and then it's not until the end of April that you were made aware of the sort of breakdown in process?

Yes, that's correct. Okay. Mr. Patino, that's quite a significant period of time given that the request from the committee had sort of come even in later December. Mr. Derrick, do you have concerns about that fact? Basically, this committee was sitting, waiting for in excess of four months for a response that had been widely circulated amongst the media.

Look, I think it's been taken very seriously. Myself and the board have made sure that through the governance teams and the communications team, this can't happen again. So it has been taken very seriously and the remedials have been put in place. I have some sympathy, and this is not an excuse, but I have some sympathy with the fact that the following days after the committee, we were inundated with media inquiries.

So our team were pretty frenetically dealing with OIAs and media, and this was missed, and that's unacceptable. It didn't help with the follow-up letter from the committee, didn't include that question and could have. And our team had assumed incorrectly that the matter had been satisfied.

But when you go through the facts, they're not in dispute and I'm satisfied that the team have taken it seriously enough that the processes in place after a meeting from this committee are quite different. In terms of the specific information that was requested, can we just now move to that? So the three questions that I asked was, what was the value of the remuneration as part of the notice period? Do you accept you've provided that information to the committee now?

What we're trying to balance here is firstly the need to ensure that the general public and the committee has information on an issue of public interest, while at the same time ensuring that we meet our responsibilities as an employer, which of course continues even after, in this case, Mr.

Dewatna's resignation. And so, the reason why we needed to go back and have a look at this further was to ensure that if we were providing further information related specifically to Mr. Dewatna's employment situation and personal information related to him, that we were able to get that balance right and not necessarily breach our obligations as an employer.

That's why when we provided information to the committee, we were able to provide with Mr. Dewatna's consent, the notice period and the salary range within which he was employed. Okay. Well, we'll look forward to that coming back to the committee. Those are all the questions I have, Mr. Chair. Thanks, Tangy. Yeah. Yeah.
